topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: Threads share a process address space but have independent execution progress and lifetime. That makes borrowing convenient and mistakes consequential: a worker can outlive the data it uses, or two workers can write the same object without synchronization. We will partition a bounded sum into disjoint ranges, give each worker a separate result slot, and join every worker before reading the combined result.

blocks.text: Concurrency begins with ownership of work and its results. Determine which data each worker reads, which state it alone writes, how its lifetime is bounded, and what event allows the caller to consume its output. The chapter’s partitioned sum is deliberately modest: it demonstrates disjoint work, bounded arithmetic, joined completion, and explicit result collection without claiming that more threads must make a small input faster.

topics.title: 16.1.1 Starting Work with std::thread
topics.summary: Constructing std::thread starts an execution associated with the supplied callable when creation succeeds. The thread object manages the association, not the entire lifetime of captured data. A joinable std::thread must be joined or detached before destruction; destroying one while still joinable calls terminate. Detaching transfers no automatic ownership of referenced objects.

blocks.text: Exceptions cannot safely escape the thread entry function into the creator’s call stack. Capture failures inside the worker and transfer them through an explicit result channel when needed. For a simple no-throw bounded arithmetic worker, keep the callable small and avoid hidden allocations or I/O. Thread creation itself can fail and must fit the surrounding resource-cleanup design.

blocks.text: A std::thread object represents a thread of execution after successful construction. The callable can begin running before the constructor’s caller reaches its next statement. Therefore, every object captured by reference must already be initialized and remain alive for the worker’s entire access period. Do not publish a pointer to partially constructed application state simply because thread construction appears near the end of a function.

Joining waits for the represented thread to complete and establishes the required synchronization with that completion. Detaching removes the local ownership handle but does not make captured references live longer or arrange result collection. It is rarely an appropriate shortcut for a bounded function’s worker tasks. (THREADS)

blocks.text: Thread construction can fail. If a loop starts several workers and a later construction throws, already-started workers still exist. The surrounding scopes must clean them up while preserving every object they use. A design that is correct only after all workers have started is incomplete. Test or reason explicitly about failure at each launch position.

blocks.text: Exceptions do not automatically travel from a worker to the creating thread. An exception escaping a thread’s initial callable results in termination. Catch within the worker and transfer an exception pointer, error value, or future result through a synchronized mechanism. The supervising thread can then join and report the failure through its ordinary error path.

blocks.text: A thread object and an operating-system thread identifier serve different purposes. The object expresses ownership and lifecycle operations; an identifier supports comparison and diagnostics. Do not use an observed identifier as permission to access another thread’s stack or shared mutable data. Correctness comes from the program’s synchronization and lifetime contracts, not from recognizing which worker probably ran first.

topics.title: 16.1.2 Managing Lifetime with std::jthread
topics.summary: C++20 jthread improves scoped lifetime management by requesting stop and joining on destruction when joinable. A worker can receive a stop_token and cooperate with cancellation, but requesting stop does not forcibly terminate arbitrary code. Blocking operations need their own wakeup or timeout integration.

blocks.text: Automatic joining prevents one common leak of execution lifetime, but it can still block indefinitely if the worker never finishes. blocks.text: std::jthread adds automatic joining and a cooperative stop mechanism to the basic thread model. When its destructor owns a joinable thread, it requests stop and joins. This simplifies ordinary scope cleanup, but it does not forcibly interrupt arbitrary work. The callable must observe the stop request or reach completion through another mechanism. A blocking native read or an unrelated condition-variable wait does not necessarily wake merely because the stop token changed. (JTHREAD, STOPTOKEN)

blocks.text: Cooperative cancellation is a protocol. Define the state changes that a stop request permits, which waits must be awakened, and whether accepted work is drained or discarded. A worker that waits on a queue may need queue closure as well as a stop request. A worker waiting on a socket may need bounded polling or an explicitly supported wakeup mechanism. Automatic join makes missing cancellation paths visible as hangs rather than repairing them.

Automatic join makes missing cancellation paths visible as hangs rather than repairing them.

blocks.text: Member and local declaration order matters. Destruction occurs in reverse order, so data used by workers must outlive the worker owners. In the partition example, partial-result storage exists before the vector of jthreads and remains alive until those jthreads have been cleared and joined. Reversing the order can leave workers accessing destroyed storage during exceptional cleanup.

blocks.text: The stop token should not become an excuse to skip invariants. A worker that notices cancellation halfway through updating shared state must leave that state in a documented condition. A bounded independent computation can often stop between complete units of work. A transaction-like operation may need to complete or roll back its local mutation before reporting cancellation.

blocks.text: For a function that returns a completed result, explicit joining before reading output is still useful even when jthread would join later during destruction. The return-value calculation can happen before local destructors execute. Relying on destructor timing while computing the result risks reading incomplete state. Join or otherwise synchronize at the point where the result becomes eligible for consumption.

topics.title: 16.2.1 Partitioning Independent Work
topics.summary: A data-parallel sum can assign each worker a disjoint input interval and one private output slot. The input is read-only, and no two workers write the same scalar result object. After all workers join, the caller combines the partial sums. This structure avoids a lock on every input element.

blocks.text: Partition boundaries must cover the input exactly once, including uneven division and fewer elements than requested workers. Empty input should have a defined result without creating unnecessary threads. Avoid vector<bool> for independent Boolean result slots because its packed representation can make distinct logical elements share a storage location relevant to concurrent modification.

blocks.text: Independent partitioning assigns each input element to exactly one worker and gives each worker a private result slot. The caller then combines those results after all workers finish. This avoids contention on a single shared sum and makes the ownership argument straightforward: input is read-only, each partial is single-writer, and final reduction occurs after joined completion.
rich: Independent partitioning assigns each input element to exactly one worker and gives each worker a private result slot. The caller then combines those results after all workers finish. This avoids contention on a single shared sum and makes the ownership argument straightforward: input is read-only, each partial is single-writer, and final reduction occurs after joined completion.

blocks.text: The quotient-and-remainder partition distributes n elements among k workers without assuming that n is divisible by k. Each worker receives either n / k elements or one additional element for the first n % k workers. Track the next beginning index and assert that the final endpoint equals n. Empty input and more requested workers than elements need explicit policies.

blocks.text: Arithmetic bounds are part of parallel correctness. Changing the order of integer additions is safe only when all evaluated operations stay within their types’ valid range. The example bounds input size and element magnitude so the partial and final long long sums remain representable. For floating-point data, different reduction orders can change rounding, so equality with a sequential result may require a defined tolerance or reproducibility policy rather than exact bitwise identity.

blocks.text: Capture the assigned range by value or store it in a stable task object. Accidentally capturing the loop’s mutable index by reference can make every worker use a later value or access an object after its scope ends. Capturing a span by value copies the view, not the underlying data; the source container must remain alive and unmodified in ways that invalidate the span.

blocks.text: Partitioning proves only the independence you actually enforce. A supposedly read-only callback that updates a hidden global cache reintroduces shared state. An element operation that accesses an external device may have ordering requirements even when the array indices are disjoint. Define the work unit’s effects, not just its input range, before declaring it embarrassingly parallel.

topics.title: 16.2.2 Understanding Scheduling Overhead
topics.summary: Creating threads, scheduling them, and combining results add work. For tiny inputs, these costs can exceed any benefit from parallel arithmetic. hardware_concurrency is a hint that can return zero; it is not a guarantee that many threads will run simultaneously or that the process has that many available cores under container or scheduler limits.

blocks.text: Choose worker count from measured workload and deployment constraints. Oversubscription, memory bandwidth, and cache effects can limit scaling. This chapter tests correctness across several worker counts but does not claim a speedup. Reusing a worker pool can reduce repeated creation cost when the application has many tasks.

blocks.text: Starting, scheduling, synchronizing, and joining threads costs work. topics.title: Failure clinic — Automatic joining at the wrong point
topics.summary: A function launches jthreads and immediately returns the sum of its partial-result vector. Local destructors join later, but the return expression already read the vector while workers were updating it. The repair is explicit completion before result evaluation. Automatic cleanup is not a substitute for a synchronization point in the algorithm.
